Orbiting Trouble: The Growing Problem of Space Junk

The rapid expansion of satellite constellations in low-Earth orbit has brought into sharp focus the long-term (22) ______ of leaving our own debris behind in space. According to the European Space Agency (ESA), about 40,000 objects are currently tracked by space surveillance networks, yet only some 11,000 of them are active satellites; the rest is junk, from spent rocket stages to fragments of past collisions. Some experts warn that a single major collision could trigger a chain reaction that would (23) ______ on the usability of entire orbits.

Compliance with mitigation guidelines is improving: roughly 90% of rocket bodies in low-Earth orbit now meet the 25-year re-entry standard. (24) ______, the debris population keeps growing, because fragmentation events add new objects faster than the atmosphere can remove them. Space agencies and regulators therefore increasingly insist that operators (25) ______ out detailed plans for retiring their spacecraft before launch. (26) ______ such obligations been in place from the outset, there would probably be far less debris circling the planet today. Without decisive action, the dream of cheap and abundant access to space may well (27) ______ up in smoke.
Adapted from ESA Space Environment Report 2025 (www.esa.int)

For most of the past century, the five-day, forty-hour week has been treated as the natural rhythm of working life. Yet a growing number of employers are questioning whether time spent at a desk (38) ______. A study published in Nature Human Behaviour in 2025 followed 141 organisations in six countries, from Australia to the United States, that cut working hours by about a fifth without reducing pay. By contrast, staff at 12 comparison companies that kept the five-day week saw no such changes.

Sceptics, however, urge caution. Because the organisations chose to take part rather than being picked at random, the results may not apply to every workplace, and not every job, whether a hospital ward or a delivery round, can simply be squeezed into fewer days. Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 43 to 50.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) arises when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites evolve to the point where the medicines once used to treat them no longer work. As a consequence, common infections become progressively harder, and sometimes impossible, to treat, which heightens the risk of wider transmission, severe illness, disability and death. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths worldwide in 2021, yet the toll is not solely clinical: current trends project treatment costs of some US$412 billion a year up to 2035, on top of productivity losses of about US$443 billion annually.
Left unchecked, resistance threatens to unravel the gains that modern medicine has made over the past century.

The principal driver of resistance is the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine, livestock rearing and crop production alike. Each unnecessary dose exerts selective pressure, allowing the few microbes able to withstand it to multiply and pass on their resistance. Poor access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene, together with weak infection control in homes, farms and health facilities, speeds up this process, while limited access to vaccines, diagnostics and medicines means that many infections are treated blindly. The burden is far from evenly spread: WHO reports that in its South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean Regions, roughly one in three reported infections is already resistant to treatment. Compounding the problem, too few new antibiotics are in development to replace those that have been

Because resistant organisms cross borders with travellers, livestock and trade, no country can contain them alone, and WHO therefore promotes a “One Health” approach that links human, animal and plant health. Its priorities include stronger surveillance and laboratory networks, better access to diagnostic tests so that antibiotics are prescribed only when truly needed, stricter infection prevention in hospitals and communities, and

access to the medicines that still work. Crucially, surveillance data reveal which pathogens are resistant to which drugs, allowing authorities to direct scarce funds towards the places where resistance is spreading fastest.
This is, however, impossible without functioning laboratories, which many low-resource settings still lack.

Ultimately, the fight against AMR is a race between microbial adaptation and human coordination. In 2024 the United Nations General Assembly set a target of cutting deaths associated with bacterial AMR by 10% by 2030, and WHO’s Global Action Plan for 2026–2036 aims to preserve effective treatments for human, animal and plant infections. One concrete goal is that, by 2030, at least 70% of antibiotic use should come from the “Access” group, which is generally less likely to fuel resistance, up from about 53% in 2022. Whether such commitments translate into practice will depend on sustained financing, accountability and political will, particularly in the countries least equipped to respond.
Adapted from WHO fact sheet “Antimicrobial resistance” (www.who.int)

runs.t: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct word or phrase that fits best each of the numbered blanks from 51 to 60.

In 1902, anxious to (51) ______ off the threat of bubonic plague, the French colonial authorities in Hanoi offered a small bounty for every rat killed in the city’s new sewers. To spare officials the (52) ______ sight of carcasses piling up at municipal offices, hunters were asked to hand in only the tails. The (53) ______ was as swift as it was perverse: inspectors began to notice tailless rats scurrying through the streets and reported rat farms on the city’s outskirts, where, it was alleged, people were breeding the animals for profit. (54) ______ on exploiting the reward, some hunters had reportedly cut off the tails and set the rats free to multiply. The bounty was eventually cancelled, and the rats remained.

Economists later labelled such backfires the “cobra effect”, after an anecdote about British-ruled Delhi that historians have never been able to verify. The Hanoi case, by contrast, is (55) ______ documented in the colonial archives. (56) ______ the figures reported by the French were often little more than guesses, the pattern they reveal is hard to dismiss.

The central (57) ______ behind such episodes was captured in 1975 by the British economist Charles Goodhart and later popularised by the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern in the words: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Once people are rewarded for hitting a number, the number comes to (58) ______ the very thing it was meant to indicate. Hospitals judged on waiting times may quietly (59) ______ their figures; schools judged on exam results may drill pupils rather than educate them. The lesson, it seems, is that wherever a number becomes an end in itself, someone will find a way to (60) ______.

Adapted from Michael G. Vann, “Of Rats, Rice, and Race: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, an Episode in French Colonial History” (French Colonial History, 2003) and World History Connected (University of Illinois Press)
Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 61 to 70.

The last wolves in Yellowstone National Park were killed in the 1920s, and for almost seven decades the park lacked its top predator. In 1995 and 1996, 31 grey wolves captured in Canada were brought back.
Few observers could have foreseen how far the return of a single predator would ripple through the ecosystem.

The most visible change concerned the elk. Counts of the northern range herd, which had exceeded 15,000 in the early 1990s, had fallen to about 6,000 by the time of a 2011 assessment, as wolves killed elk and, according to some researchers, changed where the survivors moved and how long they dared to graze.

Yet wolves were never the only factor: hunting outside the park, harsh winters and other predators such as cougars also took their toll, and some analyses attribute a far larger share of elk deaths to hunting than to wolves.

Where browsing eased, vegetation began to recover. Along four streams in the Lamar River basin, every one of the tallest young aspen shoots was browsed in 1998, compared with fewer than one in five in the most recent survey. Willows and cottonwoods began returning to some stream banks by 2006, and the number of beaver colonies in the same area rose from one in 1996 to twelve in 2009, their dams creating ponds that benefited fish and other wildlife.

Many ecologists interpreted these changes as a classic “trophic cascade”, in which a predator influences its prey, and the prey in turn shapes the plants on which it feeds. Researchers William Ripple and Robert Beschta of Oregon State University argued that the evidence of ecosystem recovery was becoming increasingly persuasive, although they cautioned that it might take decades to unfold fully and that wolves would need to reach an “ecologically effective density” to produce similar results elsewhere.

Not everyone is convinced, however. Ecologists at Colorado State University, drawing on some twenty years of data, concluded that little had changed in the willow communities along the small streams of the northern range. Their study suggested that willows depend on the high water tables created by beaver dams: when beavers abandoned their dams, the streams cut deeper channels, water tables fell and a new ecological state emerged, in which elk-grazed grassland persisted even with wolves present. The lead researcher, N. Thompson Hobbs, stressed that the work did not argue against restoring wolves, whose benefits he described as well established but possibly slow to accrue.

Both camps agree that wolves matter; where they differ is over how far, and how quickly, a predator’s return can repair an ecosystem that was altered for decades. Hunting, climate, hydrology and beaver activity all interact, and their relative weight varies from one stream to the next. The evidence is thus
on its own, and managers elsewhere who are considering restoring predators would be wise to expect uneven results that may take decades to appear.
Adapted from Oregon State University (2011), the U.S. National Park Service and The Denver Gazette (2024)
